question: Which high-frequency indicator leads official GDP data?
before: GST collections released monthly, directly reflect consumption and business activity. Available 1-2 weeks after month-end vs GDP 60 days after quarter. B is backward-looking. C is decadal. D is company-specific.
after:
Concept: A high-frequency economic indicator is one released regularly (daily, weekly, or monthly) that provides real-time or near-real-time signals of economic activity, ahead of official GDP releases which lag by 60+ days.

Why this is correct: Monthly GST collections are released 1–2 weeks after month-end and directly measure aggregate consumption and business turnover across the economy. This makes them the most timely proxy for GDP-relevant activity, allowing analysts to form views on quarterly GDP growth weeks before the official release. GST data is a leading indicator because it captures actual transaction volumes in near-real time.

Why the others are wrong: B (Annual report filings) — These are backward-looking summaries released after the financial year ends, providing no advance signal. C (Census data) — Census is conducted once every decade and is demographic, not economic activity data; it has no relevance as a leading GDP indicator. D (Company quarterly earnings) — While earnings are timely, they reflect individual company performance and accounting choices, not aggregate economic activity; they are also backward-looking for the quarter already completed.

Intuition: Equity analysts use GST collections as a live pulse of demand conditions before GDP is official. A rising GST trend suggests stronger consumption lifting corporate margins; a falling trend signals demand risk. This 6–8 week lead time is critical for repositioning portfolio exposure ahead of GDP surprises.
